exception.reason: UCR offers substantive study of Greek archaeology, ancient democracy, myth, classical rhetoric and selected ancient philosophy and history. The strongest complete combinations also require extensive general literary interpretation, modern cultural reception, philosophical debate or contemporary politics. Those subjects can form worthwhile programmes, but they do not sustain the integrated investigation of Greek and Roman texts, language, material culture and historical context that defines this Classics degree. The shortfall concerns the organising academic substance of a full programme, rather than language absence alone, a required count of matching courses or identical degree content.
exception.ucrCourseEvidence: Current workbook content independently assessed: Greek Archaeology and Heritage & Ancient Democracy directly address Greek material culture/citizenship; World Archaeology develops artefact and craft inquiry; World Myth & Literature includes Greek/Roman comparison and Ovid; Rhetorical Communication explicitly teaches Greek/Roman rhetoric. Great Literary Works includes ancient epic/tragedy among later works; Western/Political Philosophy, Empires and Ways of War include ancient sources/cases within wider histories. Literary interpretation, stylistics and art historiography offer real methods, but their general or modern objects do not become sustained Classics inquiry. No offered sequence establishes Greek/Latin textual, epigraphic and philological research. Actual course combinations were challenged before rejecting the target-level response.

candidateAssessment.label: Antiquity, democracy & the politics of the present
candidateAssessment.reason: Ancient democracy and rhetorical traditions are directly supported, and political philosophy and empire supply comparative perspectives. Expanding this into 180 EC, however, makes modern institutions, law or general philosophy the organising subject; it does not deepen the target’s integrated ancient textual and cultural inquiry. This is a different academic programme rather than a defensible full target response.

audience.programmeDescription: Classics at Radboud studies ancient Greek and Latin languages, literature and culture. Students read and translate original texts and study ancient history, archaeology and literary research.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers related courses in Greek archaeology, ancient democracy, mythology, rhetoric and philosophy. These are valuable connections, but the available courses do not support a complete programme centred on Greek and Latin language and original-text study. We therefore show Radboud’s curriculum without presenting a UCR programme as a comparable alternative.

curriculum.limitation: The 180-EC programme comprises 120 EC of required study, 30 EC of restricted Arts minors and 30 EC of open study. The pathway shown assumes school-level Greek and Latin. Where needed, language intensification replaces a first texts course. Mentorship, academic Dutch assessment and the thesis colloquium are also required zero-credit activities.

componentNotes.y2-minors: Two approved 15-EC Arts minors with fixed course packages.
componentNotes.y3-free-space: 30 EC of bachelor study outside the student’s own programme. Foreign study needs advance approval.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: Required 10-EC thesis after the two named literary and cultural methods courses; a zero-credit colloquium is also required.
componentNotes.y3-epigraphy: Requires Greek grammar 1 or 2 and Latin grammar 1 or 2.
